item.title: All gantry cranes working, port returns to regular status
item.description: All three gantry cranes at the Guam Port Authority are operational again after they were damaged by high winds on Oct. 2. The U.S. Coast Guard has also restored the port to normal operating status following Typhoon Champi.
item.content:encoded:
All three gantry cranes at the Guam Port Authority are operational again after they were damaged by high winds on Oct. 2.

The U.S. Coast Guard has also restored the port to normal operating status following Typhoon Champi.

Previously, commercial vessel traffic was allowed, but movements were restricted to daylight hours while navigational aids and harbor conditions were assessed.

Port personnel are continuing to examine facilities, equipment, marinas and waterfront infrastructure, looking for any damage caused by Typhoon Champi.

However, port officials said the assessments are taking place alongside ongoing cargo operations, so recovery efforts do not interrupt the movement of goods through the port.

Is there an area of government you think should be examined by the Guam Office of Public Accountability?

The office is asking the public for audit topic suggestions for its calendar year 2027 plan.

Suggestions may involve government programs, services, operations, use of public resources, service delivery, program administration, or other matters affecting government accountability.

You can submit your suggestions through the Office of Public Accountability’s online survey at www.opaguam.org , or by sending an email to admin@guamopa.com by Nov. 13.

item.content:encoded:
NMI Del. Kimberlyn King‑Hinds said a two‑day visit by a congressional staff delegation last week provided an important opportunity to show federal officials the progress and ongoing challenges facing the Northern Mariana Islands as the U.S. military expands its presence in the region.

King‑Hinds said the delegation — led by staff from House Speaker Mike Johnson’s office and representing members of the House Armed Services Committee — visited Saipan and Tinian to see “firsthand some of the important developments and challenges facing our islands.”

During the trip, King‑Hinds joined the group in reviewing progress on the Tinian Divert Airfield and the North Field runway project — two major Department of Defense initiatives intended to strengthen U.S. operational capacity in the Pacific.

“We also visited the Tinian power plant to see the significant damage caused by Super Typhoon Sinlaku and the challenges facing our island’s critical infrastructure,” King‑Hinds said.

She said the visit allowed for direct conversations about how federal agencies can better coordinate military development with the civilian systems that support local communities.

“As the military expands its presence in the Marianas, we have to recognize that a strong, resilient local economy and reliable public infrastructure are essential to supporting that mission,” the delegate said.

King‑Hinds said she appreciated the delegation’s willingness to travel to the islands and see local conditions.

“These are exactly the kinds of conversations we need to make sure that federal investments in our region also recognize and address the needs of the communities that support them,” she said.

item.title: Nigeria confirms an Ebola case in Abuja as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive
item.description: LAGOS, Nigeria — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said. The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.
item.content:encoded:
LAGOS, Nigeria — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. "We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the latest outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that "we are facing an extremely serious threat," with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

"This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa," he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country's preparedness for a potential outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers," the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola task force in June following the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,000 people and killed more than 4,300 people.

The latest outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said. Nigeria was one of the countries affected, recording 20 cases before it was declared over in the country after three months.

item.content:encoded:
Resilience is one of those buzzy buzzwords. But what does it mean, exactly? Bouncing back from tragedy? Conquering obstacles? Having the inner strength to follow a dream when the odds are against you?

For Dr. Vanessa Kerry, the definition is pretty straightforward. It boils down to being prepared. In the world of global health, she says, that means "strong systems, primary care and the ability to respond."

Those are the ideas that will guide her in her new job as special envoy for health resilience at the World Health Organization.

It's the latest addition to an impressive resume. Kerry was WHO's first special envoy for climate change and health, is director of global and climate health policy in the Department of Environmental Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and is the founder and CEO of Seed Global Health . That nonprofit group has been building resilience in lower-resource countries for over a decade, dispatching coaches and mentors to educate and train local healthcare students and practitioners as well as building financial and material resources.

Kerry's activism reflects seminal moments from her younger years. In grade school, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. At age 14, she traveled to Vietnam with her father, former Senator and Secretary of State John Kerry, and was deeply struck by the poverty she saw.

Between her third and fourth years in medical school, she spent time in a hospital in Rwanda. One day she was asked to "be a helping hand" with a woman's labor and delivery, working with a nurse.

Kerry said, "I'm a student." So that was the team — this medical student from the U.S. and a Rwandan nurse.

"The mother was pushing, but the baby was not advancing," Kerry remembers. "The shoulder had gotten stuck, and so we needed to do the maneuvers to help to deliver." She tried to remember everything she could from time spent in a "labor rotation a while back." There was no imaging, no specific training either she or the nurse had had for this type of situation.

"We were lucky," she says, "Because what we remembered worked." Mother and child survived.

Kerry, now 49, recalls: "I remember walking out of that room thinking, that was extremely distressing — more than that, extremely shocking and terrifying.

She could only conclude "this whole system doesn't work."

That harrowing delivery was the germ for Seed Global Health. She knew that many of her colleagues wanted to work to improve global health. But many of the opportunities involved flying in to perform certain procedures, then returning home.

"They made a contribution in that moment, but what then?"

When she returned to Boston from Rwanda to finish her residency at Massachusetts General, she began hatching the idea of working with the Peace Corps to send doctors and nurses to sub-Saharan Africa as medical educators to train health care workers who could then train others — building a country's internal health care system. Seed's collaboration with the Peace Corps lasted from 2012-2018, focusing on the development of country-led efforts at HIV/AIDS epidemic control.

Today, Seed is active in several sub-Saharan African countries for its training efforts. In Uganda, for example, Kerry says that her group has partnered with the Ministry of Health to build up emergency medicine by training 30 emergency medicine physicians. When an Ebola outbreak occurred there earlier this year, she says that these emergency physicians and other specialists were able to train over 3,000 health workers around the country in Ebola case management and infection prevention and control.

Seed, she says, has taught her that building resilience "is not a daunting task. If you train health workers, they can monitor and provide healthcare, they can provide surveillance, they can provide prevention."

Building responsive healthcare systems is what her new job is all about, she says. " We've been funding disease by disease and crisis by crisis. We can be thinking about this differently."

Her goal is not merely to jump in when a new outbreak occurs. "If a nation does not have a health system infrastructure in place, they will probably not be prepared to respond to the emergency. Resilience means building a system that will already be in place."

And it also means listening to local voices. "Countries know what their priorities are to care for their population," she says. As the resilience envoy, she wants to make sure there is ample funding so "we more effectively address the biggest burdens of disease."

Diane Cole writes for many publications, including The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She is the author of the memoir After Great Pain: A New Life Emerges. Her website is DianeJoyceCole.com

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

item.title: 'Brother of the More Famous Jack' finds its way to a new generation of readers

item.content:encoded:
I first read Barbara Trapido's sparkling coming-of-age novel Brother of the More Famous Jack when it was published in 1982. I was in my 20s, on bedrest during a difficult first pregnancy that coincided with the publication of my first novel — which was in part about a failed college relationship. Trapido's debut, about a smart-but-inexperienced young woman with a tendency to fall for the wrong guys, was just the ticket.

I loved Brother of the More Famous Jack and am freshly enamored each time it's rediscovered by a new generation and celebrated with a new edition. The latest, published in October by New York Review Books' Classics imprint, features a misleading cover photograph that transmits a melancholy vibe from the 1980s rather than swinging late '60s London, when much of Trapido's novel is set -- but don't let that put you off.

It is hard not to fall in love with Katherine Browne, Trapido's eager to please, mini-skirted narrator. In her determination to break away from her stiflingly conventional, bourgeois upbringing and forge a less constrained life, Katherine is always game for adventure. By her own admission, she's "no good at making a fuss," and considers others' shocking behavior part of her education.

Katherine finds the chaotic, profane, unabashedly carnal family of her university philosophy professor particularly instructive — and liberating. Drawn to their "bold, radical iconoclasm," she becomes infatuated with them all: the chauvinistic, leftwing patriarch, Jacob Goldman, a German Jewish refugee who later says of her college admissions interview, "The best legs I interviewed that year"; his wife, Jane, a blue-eyed madonna in Wellingtons who broke with her patrician Anglo-Irish family to marry him; and their two irreverent oldest sons, who, when exasperated, throw garlic bread at their father's head and call their mother a "dominating virago." When Katherine first visits the Goldmans on the eve of their sixth child's home birth, their conversation encompasses Jacob's graphic reasons for eschewing various methods of birth control and their small daughter's description of how the baby will arrive. A shocked but enchanted Katherine notes: "There is more sex education about than I have encountered in all my life."

Trapido was born in Cape Town, South Africa in 1941 and left for England in 1963. She was 40 when she wrote her first novel — married to an Oxford professor, raising two children, and working on a never-finished dissertation on the poetry of Dante Gabriel Rossetti. The book's 50 short, punchy chapters, packed with incident, argument, sex, and snappy dialogue, convey a delight with turmoil.

Unlike so many debuts, Trapido's is not autobiographical. Six novels have followed, three of which spin an elaborate web involving some of the same characters: Temples of Delight , Juggling and, the closest to a sequel, The Traveling Hornplayer . Her later novels, including her most autobiographical Frankie and Stankie — about two sisters growing up in cruelly racist, apartheid South Africa — are on the whole bleaker and sadder than Brother of the More Famous Jack.

Many of Trapido's novels feature close pairs of brothers or sisters, though Katherine is an only child charmed by the mess and mayhem of the Goldbergs' lively household. The brother referred to in its title is the poet William Butler Yeats (1865-1939), older sibling of the artist Jack Butler Yeats (1871-1957). It's a Goldman family joke, for who's heard of Jack Butler Yeats now? Leitmotifs in Trapido's work include classical music, Jane Austen's Emma, and Shakespeare's comedies involving mistaken identities and doubles. Other throughlines are concerns with social class, mental health, what used to be called the battle of the sexes, and love affairs both passionate and devastating.

Brother of the More Famous Jack, which the Times Literary Supplement has called "a sort of bohemian Brideshead Revisited," has become a darling of writers. Lily King calls it "literary comfort food." Rachel Cusk deems this tale of the disillusions of love "brilliantly lewd" and "hilariously satisfying." Mystery book author Mick Herron, in his introduction to this latest edition, declares Trapido's subject "the eroticism of the intellect." In the enthusiastic foreword to Riverhead's 2014 edition, Maria Semple, fresh off her own success with the charming Where'd You Go Bernadette, calls it "a thrill of contradictions...endearing and shocking... romantic and raunchy...loving and rude." Read whatever version you can get your hands on.

item.title: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses?
item.description: This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here . What if an AI bubble bursts, triggering a recession, and that recession ends up accelerating the replacement of workers with AI? Call it the AI double whammy.
item.content:encoded:
This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here .

What if an AI bubble bursts, triggering a recession, and that recession ends up accelerating the replacement of workers with AI? Call it the AI double whammy.

I've long been skeptical of sweeping claims about how AI will transform the world. I still am. We don't really know. But as this technology advances, I've found myself worrying more about what it could mean for our livelihoods.

Two strands of economic research have given me reason to take this double whammy seriously. One concerns the history of financial bubbles. The other concerns a surprising relationship between recessions and automation, when businesses use technology to do tasks that were previously done by humans.

First, the bubbles. In 1978, the economist Charles Kindleberger published an influential book titled Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises . Drawing on the theoretical work of economist Hyman Minsky, Kindleberger went through centuries of economic history and saw a recurring pattern.

Often the bubble starts with some big potential change to the economy. A revolutionary new technology, for example, that promises to transform industries and create enormous wealth. Investors have a good reason to be excited by it. But they get overly excited. During the upswing, they bet tons of money expecting basically that the sky is the limit. And they often build up debt in the process, borrowing money to make even bigger bets and thereby helping to further fuel the boom. That debt can become a ticking time bomb. When reality sets in, asset prices fall, but those debts remain. Borrowers struggle to repay, lenders suffer losses, and a market crash can spiral into a financial crisis and a painful recession.

One crucial insight is that a technology can truly be revolutionary, yet still fuel a bubble that ends in a financial crash. For example, the railroads. I wrote about that bubble in a previous Planet Money newsletter — and how its collapse triggered "The Panic of 1873." The ensuing economic turmoil helped foment a populist uprising and the first major immigration crackdown in American history.

AI is now basically propping up the U.S. stock market. An analysis from J.P. Morgan earlier this month found that just 42 AI-related companies accounted for around two-thirds of the S&P 500's stock price gains since early 2024. Meanwhile, AI-related companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to help finance data centers and the energy infrastructure to power them.

None of this proves that what we're witnessing is a bubble or that this debt is a ticking time bomb for the financial system. The bursting of the dot-com bubble helped usher in a relatively mild recession. Debt played a smaller role in that boom, helping to limit the financial fallout. Its collapse did not trigger a systemic financial crisis like the one that followed the housing market bust around 2008.

Even without a financial crisis, though, there could be a painful reckoning. Will all these companies ultimately make enough money to justify all their borrowing and spending? Will each company survive? Technology analyst Benedict Evans has warned that fierce competition between companies offering similarly capable AI models could drive down the prices they can charge and leave little room for profit — even as they're spending ungodly amounts of money to develop and run these models.

If an AI bust triggers a recession, that would be painful enough. But this is where a few studies add to my anxieties. Because they suggest that recessions can be the very moment when businesses turn to new technologies to replace workers.

We tend to imagine automation as a gradual process. Technology improves, businesses adopt it, and jobs slowly change or disappear, theoretically while new jobs appear in other parts of the economy. But this research suggests that automation can happen in bursts, and those bursts tend to cluster around recessions.

One study , by economists Nir Jaimovich and Henry Siu, found that jobs vulnerable to previous waves of automation saw most of their decline around recessions. Between 1990 and 2017, 88% of the decline in the share of Americans employed in these jobs occurred during recessions or in the months immediately before or after them.

And here's the unsettling irony: fierce price competition could keep AI companies from delivering the profits investors expect, while making their technology cheaper for other businesses to use to replace workers. If an AI bust triggers a recession, that downturn could accelerate worker replacement. Investors could lose their money, and workers could still lose their jobs.

It's a nightmare scenario. First, the bust hammers our retirement savings. Then, as businesses scramble to cut costs, many of our jobs are permanently lost.

Of course, we still don't know whether AI will deliver enough profits to justify all the borrowing and spending, whether a bust would trigger a painful recession, or whether the automation patterns found in past recessions will repeat themselves with AI. A downturn could leave businesses with less money to invest in AI. And AI could still prove more useful for helping workers get more productive than outright replacing them.

Whether AI delivers one whammy or two whammies or none, there are policies that can limit the damage when workers lose their jobs. Obviously, unemployment insurance and other policies like that. And people like Bill Gates are proposing that we should tax AI and robots , making it more economical to continue employing humans while generating revenue that the government can spend to enhance the safety net. That idea is something we might explore in a future newsletter.

So, yeah, there are reasons this nightmare might never come true, and there are ways to limit the damage if it does. That, however, hasn't stopped me from worrying about it.

But it felt cathartic writing this down — getting these worries out of my head and onto the page.

LIVE VIRTUAL EVENT FOR NPR+ SUPPORTERS Wondering what AI could mean for your livelihood? Join Adrian Ma from The Indicator from Planet Money on Wednesday, October 28, for a virtual "Ask an Economist" event about AI and jobs. It will feature Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT, and Erik Brynjolfsson, a professor at Stanford and director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. During the event, we'll invite you to share your thoughts and ask questions! This is for our NPR+ supporters, join here , and find more details on the event here .

P.S. Charles Kindleberger's life was super fascinating. As we've written before , he worked for the CIA's wartime predecessor and helped design the Marshall Plan. Someone should probably make a Hollywood movie about him.
